strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimation for interatomic potentials is an important problem, especially with scarce quantum-mechanical labels. Supporting both training from scratch and fine-tuning pretrained models is practically useful.

Empirical results are promising. On ammonia, BLIP reduces force MAE from 48.03 for the reported ensemble baseline to 41.93 ± 3.38, with ECE improving from 0.108 to 0.091 ± 0.006. Silica experiments show useful accuracy gains in the smaller training regimes and substantially better reported calibration.

Presentation: The manuscript is generally readable and provides architectural descriptions, dataset sources, training hyperparameters, and pseudocode. Experiments span a controlled particle system, an equivariant molecular potential, and a pretrained large-system model, with four seeds for BLIP.

The authors explicitly acknowledge restrictions involving MACE/UMA and distinguish deterministic prediction from stochastic uncertainty estimation in the appendix. These disclosures are useful. The application and public datasets raise no evident material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian interpretation: Section 3 starts with shared random network weights, but the approximate distributions subsequently vary by input and even by individual edge/node. The manuscript does not establish a coherent dataset-level model connecting these local distributions to a posterior over shared weights. Furthermore, the supposedly fixed prior in Eq. (9) has variance proportional to the learned posterior mean squared. This requires an explicit treatment as a learned prior or another justified model formulation; the stated standard Bayesian interpretation is insufficiently supported.

Soundness—sampling and derivation: Independent local activation sampling preserves individual activation marginals but generally removes correlations induced by shared weights across nodes and edges. Those correlations matter when messages are aggregated within one graph; Appendix D does not establish equivalence for this setting. There are also concrete inconsistencies: Eqs. (5) and (23) require a noise standard deviation proportional to sqrt(alpha), whereas Algorithm 1 uses alpha. Equation (12) omits the Gaussian KL factor of one-half and does not show the required weight-dimension aggregation. These ambiguities prevent identification of the actual optimized probabilistic model.

Uncertainty evaluation is insufficiently specified for the central calibration claim. Appendix B.2 describes averaging forces across atoms while assigning a standard deviation based on average per-atom variance. The variance of an average requires covariance information and appropriate normalization. Moreover, signed mean forces can cancel, particularly for a translation-invariant conservative potential, so calibration of this aggregate need not establish calibration of individual atomic forces. Equation (20) also calls Q a Gaussian CDF although the coverage expression requires a quantile. The implemented statistic and its physical interpretation need clarification and atom/component-level calibration checks.

Efficiency claims conflate prediction with uncertainty estimation. The deterministic mean-weight pass provides no uncertainty estimate, while the silica sample-mean experiment uses 100 stochastic passes against a four-member ensemble. Reusing the inference network does not remove repeated backbone computation. No timing, memory, or sample-count-versus-quality study supports the broad claims of minimal overhead or uncertainty estimates at no additional computational cost.

Originality and attribution of gains remain under-evaluated. The method explicitly builds on existing variational dropout and Coscia et al. (2025), making its main contribution the adaptation to interatomic potentials. There is no controlled comparison against nonadaptive Gaussian variational dropout, fixed perturbations, or a matched regularization baseline to establish the value of the input-dependent inference network. The MC-dropout comparison on the particle task alone does not resolve this.

The evidence supports narrower conclusions than those stated. There are only two chemical systems, no molecular-dynamics stability or active-learning experiment, and silica uncertainty metrics are reported only for the 1024-sample regime. Ensembles outperform BLIP on every EGNN metric in Table 1 and on silica error-ranking correlation (0.676 versus 0.602). The ammonia energy improvement is small relative to BLIP's reported variability, while baseline uncertainty across runs is unavailable. These results do not establish consistently superior or broadly trustworthy uncertainty.

Reproducibility and presentation need correction. The supplied manuscript has no usable accompanying-code link, does not clearly report MC sample counts for all uncertainty experiments or KL reduction conventions, and leaves the construction of diverse ensemble members from one pretrained checkpoint unclear. Calling posterior-mean-weight prediction a MAP estimate is unjustified, and Spearman correlation measures monotonic association rather than the claimed linear relationship. Although the implementation details are helpful, the unresolved methodological and evaluation ambiguities outweigh the empirical merits.

strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimates for interatomic potentials are practically important. Applying input-dependent variational dropout to both training from scratch and pretrained-model fine-tuning is a useful direction, especially when storing and training multiple models is expensive.

Empirical merits: On ammonia, BLIP reports lower force MAE than the ensemble baseline (41.93 ± 3.38 versus 48.03), lower ECE (0.091 ± 0.006 versus 0.108), and strong uncertainty–error rank correlation (0.863 ± 0.024). Figure 3 also shows useful silica accuracy improvements in the smaller training-data regimes.

Originality: Although the Bayesian machinery builds on existing adaptive variational dropout, its integration into message-passing potentials and pretrained ORB fine-tuning constitutes a potentially useful application contribution.

Presentation and transparency: The manuscript is generally readable, includes implementation details and pseudocode, and reports several results across four seeds. It explicitly acknowledges exclusions such as MACE and UMA, and reports cases where ensembles perform better. The impact statement is proportionate; no specific material ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian interpretation: The generative account uses network weights with a prior, but the proposed posterior varies per input, edge, and node. The manuscript does not adequately explain whether these are global model parameters or local latent variables, or derive the corresponding dataset-level objective. Moreover, the supposedly fixed prior in Equation (9) has variance proportional to the jointly optimized mean weights squared, as Equation (11) makes explicit. Such a construction needs an explicit empirical-Bayes or alternative justification; the stated derivation does not establish the claimed conventional Bayesian posterior or epistemic interpretation.

Soundness—objective and sampling inconsistencies: Equation (12) omits the one-half factor in the Gaussian KL and does not specify the weight-coordinate multiplicities or reduction needed for matrix-valued weights. More consequentially, Equations (5) and (23) use alpha as a variance multiplier, whereas Algorithm 1 multiplies the activation standard deviation by alpha rather than its square root. These specify different stochastic models. A tunable KL coefficient can absorb a global constant, but cannot resolve the sampling mismatch. The implemented objective and sampler must be clarified.

Soundness—symmetry guarantees: Section 3.3 does not establish that invariant dropout coefficients suffice for the claimed distributional equivariance. Local reparameterization with independent activation noise does not generally preserve the joint covariance induced by shared random weights. For vector-valued features, independently sampling Cartesian components can break rotational covariance even when the noise scale is invariant. The paper needs to specify which PaiNN layers are perturbed and how noise is coupled, supported by a proof or numerical symmetry tests. The footnote acknowledging samplewise symmetry breaking does not establish equivariance in distribution.

Soundness—calibration evaluation: Appendix B.2 describes ECE using forces averaged across atoms. For an isolated system with a translation-invariant energy, the total force is zero, so this averaging can cancel the very force errors that uncertainty should detect. The stated standard deviation, derived from average per-atom variance norms, is also not generally the standard deviation of the averaged force. It is unclear whether the implementation follows this description. Because calibration is a central claim, the authors should provide an unambiguous evaluation definition and componentwise or per-atom coverage results.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence: Silica sample-mean inference uses 100 stochastic forward passes, compared with four ensemble members. Evaluating the inference network once does not eliminate repeated message passing or force computation. A single pass at mean weights provides no uncertainty estimate and is not generally the predictive mean of a nonlinear network. There are no measured training-time, inference-latency, or memory comparisons, nor a sample-count versus calibration analysis. Consequently, the abstract's minimal-overhead claim and the conclusion's claim of uncertainty at no additional computational cost are unsupported.

Evaluation and originality: There is no ablation against input-independent learned variational dropout, matched Gaussian-noise regularization, or removal of the adaptive inference network, so the benefit of the principal proposed ingredient is unclear. Ammonia baselines are imported without comparable uncertainty across runs; the energy improvement over ensembles is small relative to BLIP's reported variability. EGNN ensembles outperform BLIP on all three Table 1 metrics, and silica ensembles have better uncertainty–error ranking (0.676 versus 0.602). These results support a narrower contribution than uniformly superior uncertainty and prediction. Active-learning and simulation-reliability benefits remain untested.

Reproducibility and presentation: The supplied manuscript's code-availability sentence has no URL. Although datasets and many hyperparameters are documented, Monte Carlo sample counts are not specified for every experiment, stochastic layer placement and noise sharing remain unclear, and the mathematical inconsistencies prevent a unique reimplementation. Spearman correlation is incorrectly described as evidence of a linear relationship. The acknowledged architecture limitations are appropriate, but should also qualify the architecture-agnostic framing. Overall, the promising empirical results do not outweigh unresolved issues in the central formulation, calibration evidence, and efficiency claims.

strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimation for interatomic potentials is an important practical problem. Supporting both training from scratch and fine-tuning pretrained models makes the proposed approach potentially useful, particularly when storing multiple ensemble members is expensive.

Empirical merits: The reported ammonia results are promising: force MAE improves from 48.03 for the ensemble baseline to 41.93 ± 3.38, with ECE decreasing from 0.108 to 0.091 ± 0.006. The silica experiments extend the evaluation to 699-atom structures and several training-set sizes, showing especially useful accuracy gains in the smaller-data regimes.

Originality: Applying input-dependent variational dropout to message and update functions, including pretrained force fields, constitutes a useful methodological adaptation. The contribution is primarily this integration and its empirical investigation rather than a fundamentally new variational-inference method.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable, provides algorithms, dataset sources, and substantial training details, and reports four-seed results for BLIP. Section 3.3 explicitly acknowledges architectural restrictions, and the silica discussion reports the ensemble's stronger error-ranking correlation. These are appropriate disclosures. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian interpretation: The probabilistic model does not clearly reconcile shared network weights with posterior coefficients computed separately for each edge and node. Independent local activation sampling generally does not preserve the correlations induced by shared random weights when messages are subsequently aggregated. The paper needs to specify whether weights are global or local latent variables and derive the corresponding objective. Moreover, the supposedly fixed prior in Eq. (9) depends on the optimized posterior mean parameters through θ²; an explicit empirical-Bayes or other interpretation is needed to justify the claimed Bayesian formulation.

Soundness—equations and implementation disagree: Eq. (5) specifies variance αθ², and Eq. (23) consequently requires a standard-deviation multiplier √α. Algorithm 1 instead uses α, producing variance α²θ². Appendix A.1 also omits the Gaussian KL factor of 1/2 and does not specify the weight-coordinate sums or multiplicities for matrix-valued distributions. Although a constant factor can sometimes be absorbed into the regularization coefficient, the noise-scale discrepancy changes the model itself. Without code or clarification, it is unclear which distribution and objective produced the results.

Uncertainty evaluation: Appendix B.2 describes calibration using forces averaged over atoms. Read literally, this statistic can cancel to zero for a translation-invariant conservative potential and does not establish calibration of individual force errors. The associated uncertainty aggregation also needs justification. Eq. (20) calls Q a Gaussian CDF although the comparison requires a quantile function. These ambiguities directly affect a central result; precise definitions, executable evaluation code, and component-level coverage results are needed.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence: Section 4.3 uses 100 stochastic forward passes for BLIP's sample-mean predictions, versus four ensemble members. Caching the inference network does not eliminate repeated backbone evaluations. Deterministic mean-weight inference provides no uncertainty estimate, so its baseline-like cost does not substantiate the conclusion's claim of useful uncertainty at no additional computational cost. No measured latency, memory, training-cost, or uncertainty-quality-versus-sample-count comparison resolves this distinction.

Experimental attribution and significance remain limited: There is no ablation against non-adaptive Gaussian variational dropout or comparable noise regularization, making the value of input dependence and the Bayesian objective difficult to isolate. Ammonia baselines are imported from prior work without comparable uncertainty across runs; the energy improvement, 11.71 to 11.51 ± 0.75, does not establish superiority. EGNN ensembles outperform BLIP on all three reported metrics, and silica ensembles achieve stronger error ranking (0.676 versus 0.602). The results support promise, but not uniformly superior uncertainty or demonstrated downstream active-learning utility.

Reproducibility and claim precision: The code-availability sentence ends without a link. Monte Carlo sample counts are not specified for all experiments, and the equation–algorithm inconsistencies prevent reliable reconstruction. Calling mean-weight inference a MAP estimate and Spearman correlation evidence of a linear relationship is also misleading. Overall, the practical merits are outweighed by unresolved issues in the central probabilistic formulation and uncertainty evaluation.

strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimation for interatomic potentials is an important problem. BLIP addresses both training with scarce data and fine-tuning pretrained models, with experiments spanning particle prediction, ammonia, silica, and MATPES active learning.

Empirical merits: Ammonia force MAE improves from 48.03 for the ensemble baseline to 41.93±3.38, with lower calibration error. On MATPES, uncertainty-based selection improves energy MAE from 96.65±0.09 to 91.13±1.14 relative to BLIP with random selection, providing useful downstream evidence.

Originality: Adapting input-dependent variational dropout to message and update functions offers a potentially useful integration of existing Bayesian techniques with MLIPs. The small additional parameter count and successful deterministic prediction after stochastic training are practically attractive.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable and supplies dataset sources, architecture descriptions, hyperparameters, pseudocode, and repeated runs. It explicitly discusses restrictions on equivariant architectures and the distinction between deterministic prediction and stochastic uncertainty estimation. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian formulation: Equation 9 describes a fixed prior, but its variance depends on the jointly optimized posterior mean weights. This requires an explicit empirical-Bayes or alternative generative interpretation. Moreover, edge- and node-dependent weight distributions are not reconciled with the shared global weights introduced in Section 3.1. Consequently, Equation 8 is not adequately established as posterior inference for the stated model.

Soundness—sampling and KL inconsistencies: Equation 5 specifies weight variance αθ², whereas Algorithm 1 multiplies the activation standard deviation by α rather than √α, producing variance proportional to α². Equation 12 also omits the Gaussian KL factor of one-half and the weight-dimensional summation or its normalization. These discrepancies affect the implemented stochastic model and regularization strength; they cannot be resolved from the manuscript.

Soundness—joint distribution and symmetry: Local reparameterization preserves individual activation marginals but independent activation noise generally loses correlations induced by weights shared across nodes and edges. Because message passing combines these activations, equivalence to the stated weight-sampling model needs justification. Proposition 1 establishes equivariance for mixtures of equivariant deterministic maps, but does not establish that the implemented activation-sampling procedure satisfies its assumptions. Precise noise-sharing rules and implementation-level symmetry checks are needed.

Efficiency claims exceed the evidence: Table 6 reports deterministic BLIP inference without uncertainty, while Section 4.3 uses 100 stochastic passes for sampled predictions. Appendix E indicates roughly twice the backbone computation per stochastic pass. Storage savings are credible, but low-cost uncertainty estimation relative to a four-member ensemble is not demonstrated. Matched-quality runtime measurements and a sampling-budget study are necessary.

Evaluation and originality: There is no ablation separating input adaptation from fixed or learned input-independent Gaussian noise, the KL penalty, or ordinary stochastic regularization. The method explicitly builds on Coscia et al. (2025), but its methodological advance over that approach is not isolated. Ensemble comparisons also have limits: ammonia baselines are imported without repeated-run uncertainty, the EGNN ensemble wins every reported metric, and silica ensemble uncertainty has better error ranking despite worse calibration. Post-hoc calibrated ensemble comparisons would strengthen the central UQ claim.

Reproducibility and claim precision: No BLIP implementation is linked, sampling counts are unspecified for several experiments, and the MATPES split fractions sum to 0.94 without explanation. Metric definitions contain errors, including an extra spatial sum for scalar energy MAE and an incorrectly normalized standard deviation in Equation 31. The architecture-agnostic claim needs qualification given the acknowledged exclusions. These issues, together with the unresolved formulation and sampling problems, prevent reliable reproduction and outweigh the promising empirical results.

strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimates for interatomic potentials are practically important, particularly with scarce reference calculations and when adapting pretrained models. BLIP addresses both training from scratch and fine-tuning within a compact, single-backbone framework.

Empirical merits: The results show promising gains across several settings. On ammonia, force MAE improves from 48.03 for the reported ensemble baseline to 41.93 ± 3.38, and ECE improves from 0.108 to 0.091 ± 0.006. On silica, BLIP reports substantially better calibration than the fine-tuned ensemble. The MATPES experiment includes a useful random-acquisition control and demonstrates an additional benefit from uncertainty-based selection.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable and supplies dataset sources, training hyperparameters, architectural descriptions, pseudocode, and results across multiple seeds. Appendix A.3 usefully explains why straightforward local reparameterization is incompatible with some equivariant layers.

Originality and limitations: Applying adaptive variational dropout to pretrained interatomic potentials is a potentially useful contribution even though its main ingredients are established. The explicit acknowledgment that the current implementation excludes MACE and UMA is constructive. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian interpretation: Equation 9 describes a prior with fixed variance, but its variance depends on the jointly optimized posterior mean weights θ. This requires an explicit learned-prior or empirical-Bayes interpretation; it is not the fixed-prior Bayesian model presented. Furthermore, input-dependent distributions computed separately per node and edge are not clearly reconciled with a posterior over shared network weights. The paper needs a coherent generative model and objective before its central claims of principled Bayesian weight uncertainty are established.

Soundness—conflicting mathematical specifications: Equation 5 defines weight variance as αθ², so the local-reparameterization standard deviation should involve √α. Algorithm 1 instead multiplies the standard deviation by α, producing variance α²θ². Equation 12 also omits the Gaussian KL factor of one-half and the sum over weight coordinates, unless an unstated normalization is intended. These discrepancies affect the actual training objective and sampled predictive distribution; they cannot be resolved reliably from the manuscript.

Soundness—joint sampling and symmetry: The local-reparameterization derivation establishes activation marginals, but does not establish equivalence of the joint distribution across interacting nodes or edges. Shared random weights generally induce correlations that independent activation noise does not preserve, and graph aggregation can make these correlations consequential. Proposition 1 is valid under its assumptions, but does not by itself validate the implemented activation-sampling scheme. Precise noise-sharing rules and numerical symmetry checks, particularly for PaiNN's vector features, are needed.

Efficiency claims are insufficiently qualified: The deterministic mean-weight prediction has baseline inference cost, but supplies no uncertainty estimate. Section 4.3 uses 100 stochastic passes for sampled predictions, and Appendix E states that each stochastic pass incurs the additional mean/variance computation. Table 6 reports deterministic inference cost rather than the cost of the evaluated uncertainty estimates. The parameter-storage advantage is credible, but low-cost UQ relative to a four-member ensemble is not demonstrated. End-to-end timing and accuracy/calibration versus sampling budget would resolve this distinction.

Evaluation and originality: There is no ablation against fixed or globally learned Gaussian dropout, removal of the inference network, or removal of the KL term. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate the contribution of input-dependent Bayesian adaptation from stochastic regularization. The method explicitly follows Coscia et al. (2025), but its methodological advance over that foundation needs sharper explanation and evidence. Ensemble-based active learning and post-hoc calibrated ensemble baselines would also strengthen the practical comparison.

Claims exceed the demonstrated scope: In Table 1, the EGNN ensemble outperforms BLIP on every reported metric. On ammonia, the energy improvement over the ensemble is small relative to BLIP's seed variability, and the mixture model has better uncertainty-error rank correlation. On silica, the ensemble also has higher rank correlation, while Figure 3 shows little accuracy separation at 1024 training structures. These results support a useful tradeoff, rather than uniformly superior uncertainty estimation or predictive performance. No molecular-dynamics stability or physical-observable evaluation establishes reliability in deployed simulations.

Reproducibility and presentation remain materially incomplete: The manuscript does not provide a BLIP implementation link, a complete sampling-budget specification across experiments, or sufficient detail on the selection of KL weights and noise clamps. Equation 31 places the sample-standard-deviation normalization outside the square root, and the energy MAE definitions include an unexplained sum over spatial coordinates. Calling Spearman correlation evidence of a linear relationship is also incorrect. Combined with the sampling and KL inconsistencies, these issues prevent confident reconstruction of the reported procedure. The empirical promise does not outweigh the unresolved methodological and evidential problems.

strengths: Significance: Reliable uncertainty estimation for interatomic potentials is an important practical problem. BLIP addresses both training from scratch and fine-tuning pretrained models, with a small parameter overhead and useful evidence across particle prediction, ammonia, silica, and MATPES.

Empirical merits: Ammonia force MAE improves from 48.03 for the reported ensemble baseline to 41.93 ± 3.38, alongside improved ECE (Tables 2–3). Silica experiments show useful gains in the smaller-data settings. MATPES uncertainty-guided acquisition improves over BLIP with random acquisition, supporting the practical usefulness of its uncertainty estimates.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally readable and provides dataset links, architecture descriptions, training hyperparameters, pseudocode, and results over multiple seeds. It explicitly acknowledges the local-reparameterization limitation for MACE and UMA; this disclosure is valuable.

Originality: Combining input-dependent variational perturbations with pretrained MLIP fine-tuning is a useful application-level contribution. The distinction between weight-space perturbations and activation sampling for equivariant architectures also provides relevant methodological insight.
weaknesses: Soundness—Bayesian formulation: Equation 9 calls the prior variance fixed, but it depends on the jointly optimized posterior mean weights θ. Consequently, the KL becomes independent of those weights. This could potentially be formulated as a tied-parameter empirical-Bayes or conditional latent-variable model, but the manuscript does not establish that interpretation. Likewise, per-node/per-edge input-dependent weight distributions are not reconciled with the shared-weight generative model. These omissions undermine the central claim of principled posterior uncertainty rather than merely adaptive stochastic regularization.

Soundness—implementation and derivation disagree: Equation 5 specifies variance αθ², requiring an activation standard deviation proportional to √α. Algorithm 1 instead multiplies the standard deviation by α, producing variance proportional to α². Equation 12 also omits the Gaussian KL factor of 1/2 and does not specify the parameter-count reduction needed for a weight-matrix KL. Although a global constant can be absorbed into λ, the variance discrepancy changes the model itself. Without an identified BLIP implementation, it is unclear which method generated the reported results.

Efficiency claims are not established for uncertainty estimation. Table 6's equal inference FLOPs use deterministic mean weights and provide no uncertainty. The silica predictive sampling procedure uses 100 stochastic forward passes, whereas the ensemble has four members; Appendix E states that stochastic sampling additionally requires mean and variance computation. Thus the storage advantage and deterministic prediction efficiency are credible, but low-cost UQ relative to ensembles is not demonstrated. Matched-budget timing and uncertainty-quality-versus-sample-count results are needed.

Evaluation does not sufficiently isolate the proposed contribution. There is no matched ablation against fixed or learned input-independent Gaussian perturbations using the same objective and sampling budget, so the value of adaptive inference remains unclear. Ammonia baselines are imported from prior work without comparable variability estimates, and there is no post-hoc calibrated ensemble comparison. Results are also mixed: the EGNN ensemble wins all three metrics in Table 1, ensembles have higher uncertainty–error rank correlation on silica, and Figure 3 shows nearly indistinguishable accuracy at 1024 training configurations. These results support usefulness more narrowly than the repeated superiority claims.

Reproducibility and UQ definitions need correction. Appendix B.2 describes calibration using per-structure mean forces; averaging signed atomic forces can cancel physically meaningful errors, so the exact aggregation and component-level coverage must be clarified. Equation 31 places the sample-variance normalization outside the square root. Sampling counts are not consistently specified across experiments, and the MATPES split fractions sum to 0.94 without explaining the remaining data. These ambiguities materially affect reproduction of the main uncertainty and active-learning results.

Presentation and scope: Calling the method architecture-agnostic overstates the implemented scope given the explicitly acknowledged exclusions. Evaluating posterior mean weights is not generally a posterior MAP estimate, and Spearman correlation does not establish a linear relationship. The approach substantially builds on variational dropout and the cited adaptive framework of Coscia et al. (2025), making the missing adaptation ablations especially consequential for originality. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by unresolved methodological and evidential issues.
